**CHAPTER 1**

**From Traditional Practice to**  
**Intelligent Statecraft**

*Diplomacy in the Age of AI*

*Diplomacy has always adapted to new instruments of communication and analysis. The central question is not whether technology changes diplomatic practice, but how the profession preserves judgement, trust and national purpose while it does so.*

# **Introduction**

Diplomacy is often associated with ceremony, carefully drafted communiqués and negotiations conducted behind closed doors. Yet beneath these visible forms lies a practical profession built around a small number of enduring tasks: representing the state, interpreting the intentions of others, protecting national and citizen interests, negotiating agreements, communicating policy and strengthening relationships over time. The instruments used to perform these tasks have changed repeatedly. The telegraph shortened distance; telephone and air travel accelerated consultation; email and the internet widened access to information; social media moved foreign ministries into a continuous public conversation. Artificial intelligence (AI) is the latest stage in this longer evolution, but it is distinctive because it can participate directly in the production, organisation and interpretation of information.

For diplomacy, this matters because information is not merely an input. It is part of the craft itself. A diplomat must decide which facts are credible, which signals are politically meaningful, how a phrase will be understood by a counterpart, and when ambiguity is useful rather than dangerous. Digital and AI tools can compress the time required for research, drafting, translation and monitoring. They can also help officers compare perspectives, generate scenarios and rehearse possible negotiating positions. Their value, however, depends on their relationship with professional judgement. Bjola (2018) cautions against imagining digital technologies as substitutes for diplomacy: they can change how representation, communication and negotiation are performed, but relationship-building and the negotiation of values and interests remain fundamentally human activities.

This chapter traces that continuity and change. It begins with the legal and institutional foundations of conventional diplomacy, before examining the digital turn and the emergence of AI in everyday diplomatic work. It then considers four areas in which AI may augment statecraft: policy coherence, scenario analysis, strategic communication and negotiation preparation. The chapter draws primarily on the project’s survey of 64 diplomatic officers and interviews with experienced Malaysian diplomats, alongside the attached research materials. The argument is deliberately practical: intelligent statecraft does not mean replacing diplomatic judgement with machine output. It means using new analytical capabilities to enlarge the diplomat’s field of view while retaining clear human responsibility for interpretation, choice and representation.

# **1.1 Conventional Diplomacy: Foundations of Statecraft**

Conventional diplomacy rests on an institutional architecture that predates digital technology. Article 3 of the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations identifies functions that remain recognisable in contemporary foreign ministries: representing the sending state, protecting its interests and those of its nationals, negotiating with the receiving state, ascertaining conditions and developments by lawful means, reporting to the home government and promoting friendly relations (United Nations, 1961). These functions are not relics of an analogue age. They provide the baseline against which later technological change should be assessed. AI may alter how a diplomat gathers information or prepares a brief, but it does not itself determine whom the diplomat represents, what interests should be protected or what compromises are politically acceptable.

Bilateral relations illustrate this continuity. Embassies maintain channels with host governments, cultivate political and economic networks, prepare official visits and interpret local developments for headquarters. Much of this work depends upon accumulation rather than single transactions: trust built over repeated meetings, knowledge of personalities and institutions, and the ability to recognise when formal language conceals a change in political mood. Contemporary leaders’ retreats and foreign-minister consultations remain structured around these conventional practices, even when their outcomes are distributed instantly through digital channels (Ministry of Foreign Affairs Singapore, 2025). The form may be more visible and faster, but the diplomatic relationship still depends on continuity, reciprocity and follow-through.

Treaty negotiation makes the professional character of diplomacy especially clear. The United Nations Treaty Handbook describes a formal pathway that can involve adoption, signature, ratification or accession, reservations, entry into force, depositary action and registration (United Nations Treaty Section, n.d.). Behind those legal stages lies bargaining over substance and language. Drafting is therefore not simply an exercise in producing elegant text. A single modifier, definition or punctuation mark can alter the range of obligations or preserve necessary room for manoeuvre. This is why negotiating expertise develops through repeated exposure to institutional language and to the preferences of other parties.

Consular work is the citizen-facing counterpart to high-level statecraft. The Vienna Convention on Consular Relations provides the legal foundation for protecting nationals, issuing passports and travel documents, assisting citizens, performing certain civil and notarial functions and supporting commercial and cultural relations (United Nations, 1963). Protocol, meanwhile, makes interstate interaction predictable: accreditation, precedence, credentials, official visits, flags, ceremonies and forms of correspondence reduce unnecessary ambiguity. Together, bilateral engagement, treaty practice, consular protection and protocol create the disciplined routines on which diplomatic credibility depends.

***Table 1.1  Continuity and technological augmentation across core diplomatic functions***

| Function | Conventional practice | Digital shift | Potential AI augmentation |
| ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- |
| Bilateral relations | Embassy reporting, official visits, relationship-building | Email, video links, online public diplomacy | Rapid synthesis of reporting, issue mapping, briefing support |
| Treaty negotiation | Drafting, bargaining, legal review, consensus-building | Shared digital drafts, real-time coordination | Option generation, comparison of formulations, rehearsal of counterpart arguments |
| Consular work | Citizen protection, documentation, crisis assistance | Online portals, alerts, remote communication | Triage support, information retrieval, multilingual assistance |
| Protocol | Credentials, precedence, formal correspondence, ceremony | Digital scheduling and workflow systems | Checklist support, document preparation, anomaly detection |

# **1.2 The Evolution of Diplomatic Practice**

The evolution of diplomacy is therefore better understood as layering than replacement. New technologies enter an established professional culture and gradually alter expectations about speed, visibility and the amount of information an officer is expected to process. Dato’ Mohd Suhaimi Jaafar recalled that early diplomatic training relied heavily on books, basic drafting instruction, observation and mentoring. Junior officers learned by accompanying senior diplomats to meetings, listening to speeches and gradually acquiring the ‘terms of art’ of negotiation. In his assessment, that method still has value because diplomatic skill is learned through practice rather than through information alone.

*“Dulu punya style, coaching, mentoring is very important because there are certain skill yang you need to learn over time.”1*

What has changed is the environment surrounding that apprenticeship. Dato’ Suhaimi repeatedly returned to the importance of speed: international events evolve continuously, public expectations move quickly, and an internal government clearance chain can itself consume valuable time. A young officer is now expected not only to understand a file but also to locate information rapidly, produce concise drafts, follow developments across multiple channels and respond to audiences that may already have encountered the issue online. Technology does not remove the need for experience; it increases the premium on knowing what deserves attention.

Ambassador Zamshari Shaharan described a parallel transformation in external communication. Earlier in his career, officers were often discouraged from speaking to the media. Over time, however, foreign ministries became more engaged with journalists and later with social-media audiences. During Malaysia’s ASEAN chairmanship, he observed how strategic communication became more central to interactions with senior leadership and the Prime Minister’s Office. The change is significant: ministries increasingly seek to shape an information environment proactively rather than simply respond after a narrative has taken hold.

*“Masa media ni, is something that we say no. You are not supposed to speak to the media. ... But that has changed.”2*

These accounts point to an important distinction between tradecraft and tools. The professional core \- judgement, discretion, relationship-building, linguistic sensitivity and accountability \- develops slowly. The surrounding tools change quickly. Diplomatic institutions therefore face a dual obligation: preserve the experiential learning through which officers acquire judgement, while modernising the information practices through which that judgement is exercised.

# **1.3 The Digital Turn in Diplomacy**

The digital turn made diplomacy more immediate, public and networked. Foreign ministries could communicate directly with international and domestic audiences, while leaders’ statements, images and policy signals circulated without waiting for the traditional news cycle. Dato’ Suhaimi described this shift in simple terms: ‘the optics, the content, the message’ have become more important because social media operates continuously. The same policy position may still be communicated privately through a diplomatic note, publicly through a press statement and conversationally through a social-media post; each form requires a different level of detail and a different tone.

This shift also changed the meaning of public diplomacy. Bjola (2018) argues that digital tools are most useful when they are connected to clear foreign-policy objectives, target audiences and measures of effectiveness. Merely creating more content does not constitute strategy. The diplomatic value of a platform depends upon whether it helps a ministry represent interests, understand audiences, build relationships or influence an issue in ways that support policy. This is a useful bridge to AI: the danger is not only technical error, but the possibility that sophisticated tools are used without a strategic question to answer.

The digital turn has also expanded the quantity of relevant information. Diplomats now operate amid official statements, social-media reactions, live news, data dashboards, messaging platforms and rapidly circulating commentary. This can improve situational awareness, but it also creates cognitive congestion. The challenge increasingly lies in selection: identifying what is authoritative, what is novel, what reflects a genuine shift in behaviour and what is simply noise. AI enters diplomacy at precisely this point, promising to make large information environments more searchable and compressible.

# **1.4 The Emergence of AI in Diplomatic Practice**

A useful contemporary definition describes an AI system as a machine-based system that infers from the inputs it receives how to generate outputs such as predictions, content, recommendations or decisions, with systems differing in autonomy and adaptiveness after deployment (OECD, 2024). In diplomatic practice, the relevant category is broad. It includes generative tools used for drafting and summarisation, translation systems, search assistants, sentiment and media-monitoring tools, forecasting applications, pattern-detection systems and analytic platforms that can organise large collections of documents. The common feature is not that these tools ‘think’ like diplomats, but that they can transform inputs into outputs that may influence a diplomat’s next step.

The project survey suggests that these tools are already associated with substantial perceived gains. Among 64 respondents, 89.1 per cent agreed or strongly agreed that AI can facilitate real-time monitoring of international trends; 87.5 per cent agreed that AI can enhance analysis of geopolitical and strategic issues; 85.7 per cent of valid respondents said it had optimised productivity; and 82.8 per cent considered AI significant in enhancing their overall effectiveness (Survey for Diplomats, 2026). Open-ended responses show that officers most commonly use AI for information gathering and research, faster drafting and language refinement, summarisation, synthesis and routine administrative work. Some respondents also described using it to identify blind spots, consider hypothetical scenarios or support negotiation preparation.

***Figure 1.2  Survey findings: perceived contribution of AI to diplomatic work***

![][image2]

*Note: Agreement combines “Agree” and “Strongly Agree”. n \= 64, except productivity (n \= 63 valid responses).*

These findings should not be read as evidence that adoption is uniform. The survey did not ask a single binary question about whether an officer ‘uses AI’, and several respondents reported limited personal use even while expressing positive expectations. The more defensible conclusion is that AI has entered diplomatic workflows unevenly but meaningfully. Its strongest early foothold is in preparatory work \- searching, summarising, drafting and checking \- rather than in autonomous decision-making. That pattern is consistent with the interviews. Ambassador Zamshari argued that the technology cannot simply be avoided: ‘we have to embrace, we have to use’. At the same time, he stressed that prior foreign-policy knowledge remains necessary to verify and contextualise what a system produces.

The experience of other foreign ministries points in the same direction. Singapore’s Foreign Minister has publicly described the problem of cognitive overload in diplomacy and the usefulness of large language models for analysis, abstraction, drafting and preparation, while emphasising that such tools augment rather than remove human responsibility (Ministry of Foreign Affairs Singapore, 2026). The practical lesson is that AI is likely to become embedded not through one dramatic automation of diplomacy, but through many small reductions in the friction of everyday work.

# **1.5 AI for Policy Coherence and Inter-Ministerial Coordination**

Foreign policy rarely belongs to a single ministry. Trade, defence, digital policy, climate, migration, energy, health and investment all have international dimensions, and major diplomatic decisions often require positions to be reconciled across agencies. The difficulty is not only obtaining information from each institution; it is recognising inconsistent assumptions, outdated language or competing definitions before they reach senior decision-makers. AI can support this coordination by comparing briefs, extracting commitments, identifying points of divergence and producing structured issue maps for human review.

This is an area where the value of AI depends strongly on institutional architecture. A model can compare documents only if it is allowed to access them, and the resulting synthesis is only as authoritative as the data and instructions supplied to it. The OECD’s 2026 Digital Government Outlook notes that governments are increasingly adopting AI but still face uneven delivery capabilities, interoperability and governance, and recommends shared digital infrastructure, clear accountability, reliable data and systematic evaluation (OECD, 2026). For foreign ministries, this implies that inter-ministerial AI should be designed around approved sources, access controls and traceable ownership rather than around informal copying of sensitive material into public tools.

Used appropriately, the technology can reduce coordination costs without replacing coordination itself. A cross-ministry policy team could ask an approved system to compare national statements, legislation and negotiating mandates; flag where terminology differs; and produce a question list for officials to resolve. The AI is useful because it surfaces potential inconsistencies quickly. The decision about which position prevails remains political and institutional. Policy coherence is therefore a good example of intelligent statecraft: machines can help reveal the shape of a problem, but they cannot settle the underlying distribution of authority or national priorities.

# **1.6 AI-Assisted Policy Simulation and Scenario Analysis**

Diplomats routinely work under uncertainty. A proposed sanction may alter supply chains; an election may change a partner’s negotiating posture; a crisis can produce second- and third-order consequences that are difficult to anticipate. Scenario analysis helps officials think beyond a single forecast by asking how different combinations of drivers could develop and what a policy would look like under each plausible future. AI can assist this process by generating alternative scenarios, organising assumptions, identifying variables that have been overlooked and comparing how a policy performs across different conditions.

This use should be understood as structured exploration rather than machine prediction. UNDP’s recent foresight guidance explicitly distinguishes foresight from predicting the future and recommends methods such as horizon scanning, scenarios, implications analysis, backcasting and wind-tunnelling or stress-testing (United Nations Development Programme, 2026). AI can make those methods easier to iterate: an analyst can ask for alternative assumptions, adversarial interpretations or consequences for different stakeholders. The gain lies in the breadth and speed of exploration, not in treating generated scenarios as probabilities.

Survey responses already hint at this emerging practice. One officer wrote that AI had enabled a broader perspective by helping to consider ‘diverse hypothetical scenarios’ and potential outcomes; another described using AI to monitor trends and prepare scenarios. These are useful applications because they challenge the analyst to consider more than the most obvious path. The discipline, however, remains human: diplomats must decide which assumptions are credible, which interests matter and how much weight to give weak signals. In scenario work, AI is best used to widen the question set before officials narrow the policy choice.

# **1.7 Data-Driven Strategic Communication**

Strategic communication has moved from an auxiliary function to an increasingly central component of diplomatic practice. Ministries must explain policy to domestic audiences, communicate with foreign publics, correct misleading narratives and ensure that official messages are timely enough to remain relevant. The interview with Ambassador Zamshari illustrates how this has changed internal workflows. His division increasingly plans communications around visits and major events, coordinates with desk officers and senior leadership, and seeks media-monitoring and sentiment-analysis capabilities that can show whether public responses are positive, negative or neutral.

AI can strengthen this work in three distinct ways. First, it can help monitor large volumes of public information and cluster recurring themes. Secondly, it can support message development by comparing how different formulations may fit different platforms or audiences. Thirdly, it can accelerate production by turning approved facts and key messages into first drafts, summaries, captions or briefing lines. These uses are particularly valuable when officials must respond within hours rather than days. Yet speed should not be confused with persuasion. A model may produce grammatically polished text without understanding why a phrase carries political sensitivity or why a particular audience will distrust a given framing.

Dato’ Suhaimi’s emphasis on narrative is therefore important. He described the contemporary environment as a ‘battle of narratives’ and argued that diplomats must know how to marshal an argument rather than merely assemble facts. AI can help with wording, structure and alternative formulations, but the diplomat still decides what the state is trying to say, to whom, and with what degree of openness or ambiguity. Strategic communication becomes intelligent not when every message is machine-optimised, but when data and AI make human communicators more aware of audiences while institutional judgement controls the final message.

# **1.8 AI-Assisted Negotiation Preparation**

Negotiation preparation is perhaps the clearest example of AI’s potential to support rather than replace diplomatic craft. Before a negotiation, an officer must understand the issue, the national mandate, the counterpart’s likely interests, relevant precedents, red lines and possible zones of agreement. AI can accelerate the preparatory stage by summarising documents, constructing issue matrices, generating counterpart questions, comparing draft clauses and simulating arguments from different positions. Several survey respondents explicitly identified this opportunity. One noted that AI could simulate different negotiating scenarios, while another suggested using it to anticipate questions that the other party might raise.

The boundary becomes visible when preparation turns into negotiation itself. Dato’ Suhaimi’s account of ASEAN drafting emphasised how consensus emerges from a baseline text, negotiated strengthening and careful treatment of new elements. He also stressed that diplomatic language contains layers that general-purpose systems may not recognise. His example was the difference between referring to ‘Myanmar authorities’ in ASEAN parlance and using a more politically charged label in another context. The issue is not simply linguistic correctness. Word choice can signal recognition, distance, solidarity, legal interpretation or room for future compromise.

AI-assisted preparation is therefore most valuable when it is adversarial and comparative. Rather than asking a system for ‘the best negotiating position’, a diplomat can ask it to generate several plausible counterpart arguments, identify weaknesses in the home position, propose alternative formulations and test how each might be interpreted. The officer can then verify those possibilities against institutional memory, legal advice and knowledge of the counterpart. This keeps the model in the role of rehearsal partner rather than negotiating authority.

The larger implication is that AI may actually increase the value of experienced diplomats. If routine synthesis and first-draft production become cheaper, comparative advantage shifts towards abilities that are harder to automate: reading intention, building trust, recognising culturally specific signals, deciding when to concede, and accepting responsibility for a national position. As Ambassador Zamshari put it when asked about the future significance of diplomats in an AI-enabled environment: ‘More. I would say more’. The technology raises the standard for preparation; it does not remove the human burden of representation.

# **Conclusion**

Diplomacy has never been technologically static. Its institutional foundations remain anchored in representation, negotiation, consular protection and protocol, but each communications revolution has altered the tempo and reach of those functions. The digital turn made diplomacy more public and continuous; AI now adds a capacity to search, synthesise, generate and compare information at a scale that changes how preparatory work can be organised. The survey data show that diplomats already associate AI with faster monitoring, improved productivity and more efficient analysis. The interviews reveal a similar acceptance of technological change, but they also draw a firm line around judgement, nuance and responsibility.

The practical value of AI is therefore greatest where it expands human capability. It can help ministries compare positions across agencies, explore alternative scenarios, monitor public narratives and rehearse negotiations. In each case, the system provides speed, breadth or structure; the diplomat supplies the mandate, context and decision. This division of labour is not a temporary compromise until machines become more capable. It reflects the nature of diplomacy itself. Statecraft is not only information processing. It is the authorised representation of interests between people and institutions whose choices carry political consequences.

Intelligent statecraft should thus be understood as a professional model rather than a technological destination. A capable diplomatic service will combine secure AI tools with institutional memory, specialist knowledge, disciplined verification and continuing human contact. Officers will need to know both how to use AI and when its apparent efficiency conceals a loss of context. The result should not be diplomacy conducted by machines, but diplomacy in which technology gives humans more time and analytical space to do what the profession has always required: understand, persuade, negotiate and exercise judgement on behalf of the state.

2.0  REAL-WORLD AND POTENTIAL AI RISKS IN DIPLOMACY

Real-World and Potential AI Risks in Diplomacy

Artificial intelligence has significantly improved diplomatic work through tools that promise speed, reach and analytical convenience. One cannot deny that these benefits are tangible. Officers hardly need to read thick documents one by one, or manually sift through scores of data before writing a report. One can now scan large quantities of information, obtain a first draft, compare positions and monitor rapidly changing narratives in a fraction of the time previously required. This process has been argued to have significantly increased the efficiency and efficacy of work. Yet the same capabilities create new points of vulnerability. A seemingly “polished” draft can conceal an error; a voice of someone in authority can be synthetically reproduced to deceive others; and portions of apparently harmless data can reveal sensitive patterns when aggregated. The central issue is therefore not whether AI is useful to diplomacy, as one cannot deny that it is. Rather, the real question is *how* the use of AI changes the conditions under which trust, judgement and state responsibility are exercised.

Many of the risks discussed in this chapter are not entirely new, yet the reach and adverse impact of these risks are much greater. Disinformation, political interference, impersonation and espionage have long contributed to the volatility of international relations. What generative AI changes, however,  is the speed and scale of these harmful practices. The related problems become that much harder to detect and address due to how AI can make completely false scenarios entirely plausible.  How can a harm be mitigated, when one is not able to identify it until it is too late?

The International AI Safety Report 2026 supports the fact that advanced AI can aggravate existing harms and that important failure modes may only become visible in real-world use (International AI Safety Report, 2026). For foreign ministries, the problem is exacerbated if the problem results in complications–the effects of which can be felt not only within our shores, but may also strain our relationship with other countries.

The chapter explores the immediate problem of diplomatic misunderstanding to wider risks involving information integrity, elections, data and national security. The chapter then extends to the perceptions of serving diplomats in Malaysia regarding \*\*\*. Whilst we do not negate that adaptation and adoption of emerging  technologies is important for us to stay ahead, employing the technology without awareness as to its limitations and related risks may not translate into the strategic impact we desire. Therefore, this chapter has identified certain vulnerabilities related to the usage of AI that one must be cognisant of, particularly in the world of diplomacy, whilst also outlining the necessary safeguards that put human judgment in the forefront of the work that we do.

![][image4]

*Figure 2.1  From AI capability to diplomatic consequence: a simplified risk pathway.*  
 *Source: Authors’ synthesis based on the chapter evidence.*

**2.1  AI-Enabled Diplomatic Misunderstandings and Misjudgement**

Diplomacy is particularly sensitive to context. A sentence that is harmless in one setting may be provocative in another; a technically accurate translation may still be diplomatically inappropriate; and an omitted qualification can alter the apparent meaning of a national position. Generative AI is vulnerable to these problems because it produces plausible language without independently understanding the political significance of every phrase it generates. In diplomatic work, an incorrect office-holder, an outdated border description, a mistranslated legal term or a fabricated source can carry consequences far beyond an ordinary drafting mistake.

Several attached cases show how confident but incorrect outputs can pass through professional workflows. In 2025, an AI-generated summer reading list containing invented books by real authors was published by major newspapers; only five of the fifteen titles were genuine (Blair, 2025). A separate Australian case involved a government-commissioned Deloitte report that was corrected after non-existent academic references and an invented judicial quotation were identified; the firm acknowledged the use of generative AI in the production process (Tadros & Karp, 2025; Croft, 2025). These were not diplomatic incidents, but the mechanism is directly relevant: fluency can create an appearance of authority that discourages scrutiny.

The consequences become more immediate when AI is used for practical advice concerning politically sensitive jurisdictions. A 2026 report described Israeli travellers who said they relied on an AI chatbot indicating that transit through Kuala Lumpur would be safe, only to be detained at Kuala Lumpur International Airport (Malay Mail, 2026). The episode required diplomatic intervention and illustrates a simple but important rule: authoritative questions on entry restrictions, sanctions, consular access, territorial issues and crisis advisories must be checked against primary government sources. In these areas, “likely correct” is not an adequate standard.

Misjudgement can also arise without a factual hallucination. An AI system may summarise a document accurately but flatten its hierarchy of importance; it may translate words correctly while missing diplomatic nuance; or it may privilege a dominant international narrative that does not reflect a country’s policy position. Dato’ Mohd Suhaimi Jaafar’s interview offers a concrete example of why diplomatic parlance matters: a term that may be acceptable in public discourse can be inappropriate in an ASEAN negotiating context. The lesson is that human review is not a ceremonial check at the end of an automated process. It is the point at which institutional memory, protocol, political sensitivity and national interest are reintroduced into the work.

**2.2  Misinformation, Disinformation and Deepfake Impersonation**

Misinformation and disinformation are related but distinct. Misinformation is false or misleading information circulated without necessarily intending to deceive; disinformation involves deliberate manipulation. AI complicates the boundary because a user may unknowingly pass on a model-generated falsehood, while another actor may intentionally use the same technology to fabricate evidence, imitate a trusted person or automate persuasive messaging. For diplomats, the distinction matters because accidental error may call for correction, whereas deliberate manipulation may require attribution, security investigation, strategic communication and coordination with platforms or law-enforcement bodies.

Deepfakes intensify the problem by weakening familiar signals of authenticity. RAND’s primer on AI, deepfakes and disinformation shows how synthetic video, voice, image and text can support influence activity in already-fragmented information environments (Helmus, 2022). The European Parliamentary Research Service similarly describes the information sphere as a contested geostrategic space in which generative AI can make manipulation cheaper, faster and easier to localise across languages (Bentzen, 2025). The difficulty is not confined to believing a fake. Once synthetic media becomes commonplace, authentic evidence can also be dismissed as fabricated, creating what is often called the “liar’s dividend”.

Two attached cases move this risk from theory to direct impersonation. In Indonesia, deepfake videos appearing to show President Prabowo Subianto promoting a financial-aid scheme circulated widely and were linked to scams affecting victims in multiple provinces (The Straits Times, 2025). In the United States, an impostor used AI-driven technology to pose as Secretary of State Marco Rubio and contact foreign ministers and other officials by text, Signal and voicemail (Lee, 2025). The latter is particularly significant for diplomacy because it targets the trust architecture of official communication itself. A convincing voice message, familiar name or plausible style can no longer be treated as sufficient proof of identity.

The security response must therefore be procedural as well as technical. Sensitive requests, unusual instructions and urgent messages should be authenticated through known channels, call-back procedures and institutional contacts rather than through the medium in which the request first arrives. Detection tools can assist, but they should not be the sole line of defence. (Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency \[CISA\], 2023\) advises organisations to combine technical detection with verification procedures and response planning for synthetic-media threats. In diplomatic settings, the practical equivalent is layered authentication: secure channels, independent confirmation, trained scepticism and rapid clarification when fabricated content enters the public information space.

**AI Risk Pathways in Diplomatic Practice**

| Risk pathway | AI mechanism | Diplomatic consequence | Primary safeguard |
| ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- |
| Hallucination or stale output | Plausible but false, outdated or decontextualised content | Incorrect brief, advice, interpretation or public statement | Primary-source verification; named human reviewer |
| Synthetic impersonation | Voice cloning, deepfake video or fabricated messages | False instructions, compromised contacts, reputational damage | Out-of-band authentication; secure call-back procedures |
| Automated influence | Low-cost generation and localisation of persuasive content | Narrative manipulation, public pressure and bilateral friction | Strategic communication; monitoring; rapid correction |
| Data inference or leakage | Prompts, uploads or aggregation reveal sensitive relationships | Exposure of policy positions, networks or vulnerabilities | Data classification; secure deployment; access controls |

*Table 2.1  Illustrative pathways through which AI-related risks can affect diplomatic practice. Source: Authors’ synthesis of attached project materials.*

**2.3  Political and Electoral Interference**

Political interference is one of the areas in which AI’s capacity for scale matters most. Influence operations existed long before generative AI, but automated content generation lowers the time and expertise required to produce persuasive text, images, audio and video for different audiences. It also enables rapid experimentation: the same narrative can be translated, reframed and redistributed to exploit local grievances, political cleavages or uncertainty. Bentzen (2025) argues that generative AI can accelerate foreign information manipulation and interference by making content production and adaptation more efficient.

Electoral interference should not be imagined only as a dramatic deepfake released immediately before polling. It can involve fabricated endorsements, cloned candidate voices, false claims about voting procedures, synthetic grassroots accounts, narrative laundering and large volumes of low-cost material intended to exhaust fact-checkers or create doubt. The Indonesian experience demonstrates how the same synthetic-media capability can move between political communication and criminal exploitation. Deepfake techniques that featured during the 2024 presidential campaign were later repurposed in scams using President Prabowo’s likeness (The Straits Times, 2025). The technology is transferable even when the motive changes.

The diplomatic implications arise because election interference can cross borders quickly. Foreign ministries may be required to respond when manipulated content is attributed to another state, when diaspora communities are targeted, when a false statement is placed in the mouth of a foreign leader, or when synthetic media threatens bilateral relations. The challenge is intensified by compressed decision time: governments may feel compelled to respond before provenance is established, thereby amplifying the falsehood they are trying to counter. (Federal Bureau of Investigation & CISA, 2024\) warned that foreign threat actors may use multiple tactics to develop and spread disinformation around elections, including fabricated content intended to undermine public confidence.

This does not mean that every AI-generated political artefact changes voter behaviour or strategic outcomes. Evidence of capability, exposure and impact must be distinguished. The policy objective is therefore resilience rather than panic: pre-agreed coordination between foreign affairs, election authorities, cybersecurity agencies, law enforcement and strategic-communication teams; rapid mechanisms for authenticating official statements; and clear thresholds for when an online falsehood becomes a diplomatic or national-security issue. Such arrangements reduce the risk that institutions improvise roles during a crisis.

**2.4  Threats to Data, Cybersecurity and National Security**

Data risk is broader than the accidental uploading of a classified document. Contemporary AI systems can infer sensitive information from combinations of apparently low-sensitivity material. Wang et al. (2025) describe “data inference” as the extraction of critical information from less sensitive data and argue that AI’s ability to combine heterogeneous sources, identify complex relationships and search large combinatorial spaces weakens assumptions that once supported traditional data-classification practices. For diplomacy, this matters because travel patterns, meeting schedules, biographies, procurement records, public statements and mission activity may reveal sensitive patterns when analysed together.

Cyber risk is also changing as AI lowers barriers for reconnaissance, social engineering, vulnerability research and the processing of stolen information. The United Kingdom’s National Cyber Security Centre assesses that AI is likely to make elements of cyber intrusion more effective and efficient and to increase the frequency and intensity of cyber threats, while AI adoption itself can expand the attack surface (National Cyber Security Centre, 2025). The International AI Safety Report 2026 similarly records rapid advances in AI-enabled cyber capabilities while emphasising persistent uncertainty about how reliably more autonomous systems can carry out complex attacks (International AI Safety Report, 2026).

Diplomatic networks are attractive targets because they contain policy assessments, negotiating positions, personal data, contact networks and privileged communications. Risk can arise even when the model itself is not compromised. An officer may disclose information through a prompt, upload an attachment to an unapproved service, use a personal account for official work, or accept a system’s suggestion to connect to an external tool without understanding the data flow. Security therefore depends on the entire workflow: approved tools, identity and access controls, logging, data-loss prevention, retention policies and clearly defined rules on what may be entered into external systems.

Malaysia’s Cyber Security Act 2024 strengthens the national framework for cyber governance, including obligations around National Critical Information Infrastructure, incident notification and risk management (PwC Malaysia, 2024). Yet AI raises operational questions that cybersecurity legislation alone does not answer for diplomatic services: Which models may officers use? What information classifications are permitted? Are prompts retained by the provider? Can foreign-hosted systems be used for restricted material? Who approves specialised tools at overseas missions? The National Guidelines on AI Governance & Ethics (AIGE) provide a broader national foundation through principles such as privacy, security, transparency and accountability, but those principles still require translation into foreign-affairs procedures (Ministry of Science, Technology and Innovation Malaysia, 2024).

**2.5  Diplomat Concerns and Threat Perceptions**

**Survey findings: leading security and operational risks**

The survey of 64 diplomatic officers provides a practitioner-centred view of these concerns. Respondents included officers at headquarters, overseas missions and IDFR/SEARCCT, with service ranging from less than five years to more than twenty-five years. Their overall assessment of AI was positive: the four-item performance-expectancy mean was 4.10 out of 5, and the belief that mastering AI-related skills adds professional value was the highest individual item at 4.36. Institutional clarity, however, was weaker. The statement that organisational procedures, rules, guidelines and limitations for AI use are clear and systematic recorded a mean of 2.50, the lowest of the sixteen Likert items. Access to expert guidance and documentation was also comparatively low at 2.84. Officers therefore appear more convinced of AI’s usefulness than of the arrangements governing its use (Survey for Diplomats, 2026).

Open-ended responses sharpen that contrast. A non-exclusive thematic coding of the “Potential Risks” question found that 46 of 64 respondents (71.9 per cent) explicitly referred to confidentiality, security, classified information, restricted documents, privacy or data leakage. Fifteen respondents (23.4 per cent) identified high-stakes decisions, negotiations, briefs, policy or crisis work; eleven (17.2 per cent) raised national interest, country positions, sovereignty or bias; ten (15.6 per cent) warned about over-reliance, verification or accountability; and five (7.8 per cent) explicitly referred to human judgement, context, empathy or diplomatic nuance. Since a single response could fall into more than one category, the percentages are not mutually exclusive. They indicate the concerns officers spontaneously prioritised rather than a ranked-choice result.

![][image5]

*Figure 2.2  Thematic coding of open-ended survey responses on work that diplomats consider risky to delegate to AI. Categories are non-exclusive; n \= 64\. Source: Survey for Diplomats: Innovating Diplomacy (Responses), 2026\.*

The responses are strikingly concrete. Officers referred to cabinet papers, situation reports, bilateral insights, negotiation positions, security updates, restricted material and assessments touching on national sovereignty. Several questioned whether foreign-hosted AI services could be trusted with government information even when enterprise subscriptions were used. Others focused on the gradual transfer of judgement to the tool. One respondent warned that officers may become “too lazy to read the entire documents” before asking AI to craft a reply or summary; another wrote that AI is “only a tool used to aid” and that officers must still dictate their work. The central fear is therefore not merely technical malfunction. It is the possibility that efficiency may erode professional control over information, judgement and accountability.

**Diplomat perspectives: trust in digital communications**

The interviews add a longer historical perspective. Datin Paduka Nur Ashikin, who joined the diplomatic service in 1994, contrasted earlier difficulties in obtaining information with the present problem of information abundance. She observed that participants can be inclined to believe AI-generated material “because it looks very professional, and very well-presented”.¹ Her conclusion was equally direct: “the human factor is still very important”.² The point is subtle but important. The danger is not only that diplomats cannot distinguish an obvious fake from a genuine document; it is that professional-looking output can borrow credibility from the conventions of official writing.

Dato’ Mohd Suhaimi Jaafar described a related transformation in the broader information environment. In his account, diplomacy increasingly takes place within a “battle of narratives”, where public communication operates alongside traditional government-to-government channels. He observed: “People don’t know what is right, what is wrong, but the most important thing is how you convince people to believe your story.”³ This is best read as a description of the contemporary information environment rather than an endorsement of manipulation. Credibility now competes with speed, repetition, emotional resonance and the ability to occupy attention. AI can help a ministry communicate more quickly, but it can also help adversaries fabricate and localise competing narratives.

Ambassador Zamshari Shaharan similarly emphasised that AI should be used in combination with prior knowledge and verification. His interview stressed the need to check AI-generated material against Malaysia’s policy position and institutional knowledge rather than treating the system as an authority in itself. The survey and interviews therefore converge on the same boundary: officers are generally open to AI as an assistant but cautious about delegating judgement where confidentiality, national interest or political consequence is high. Verification, source awareness, authentication and data discipline are becoming part of diplomatic tradecraft rather than specialist technical practices.

![][image6]

*Figure 2.3  The chapter’s central finding: AI risks converge on diplomatic trust, while effective safeguards depend on human control and institutional discipline. Source: Authors’ synthesis.*

**Conclusion**

The risks examined in this chapter share a common theme: AI weakens some of the signals on which diplomatic trust has traditionally relied. Fluent language is no longer evidence of factual reliability; a familiar voice is no longer proof of identity; and a large body of individually public data is not necessarily harmless when considered in aggregate. At the same time, the evidence does not support treating AI as inherently unsuitable for diplomacy. The diplomat survey records clear gains in research, drafting, monitoring and productivity, while interviewees repeatedly argue that the technology must be understood and used rather than ignored.

The critical distinction is therefore between assistance and authority. AI may accelerate information processing, widen the range of sources considered and support preliminary analysis, but responsibility for diplomatic judgement remains human and institutional. The practical safeguards follow from that principle: verify authoritative claims against primary sources; authenticate sensitive communications through independent channels; keep classified and restricted information within approved systems; and maintain clear accountability for outputs that influence policy, negotiation or public communication.

This approach also avoids the false choice between innovation and caution. Diplomatic services do not need to reject AI in order to protect trust, nor should they accept every efficiency gain at the expense of professional judgement. The more durable objective is to build an institutional culture in which officers understand both the capability and the limits of the tools they use. If AI is to strengthen diplomacy rather than merely accelerate it, the disciplines of verification, security and human responsibility must advance at the same pace as the technology itself.

**CHAPTER 3**

**Limitations of AI in**  
**Diplomatic Practice**

*From useful assistance to disciplined verification*

*AI can make diplomatic work faster, broader and more responsive. Its limitation is that it does not carry diplomatic memory, political accountability or human sensitivity. The task is therefore not to reject AI, but to build a professional habit of using it with caution, context and verification.*

# **Introduction**

The previous chapters established that AI is no longer peripheral to diplomacy. It is already used for research, drafting, monitoring, translation, summarisation and preparation. Yet a tool that increases speed can also widen the distance between fluency and truth. In diplomacy, that distance matters. A polished sentence may hide a weak source; a quick translation may flatten legal nuance; an apparently balanced summary may reproduce the assumptions of the data on which a model was trained. The limitations of AI therefore deserve separate treatment from the risks described earlier. Risk concerns what may go wrong in practice. Limitation concerns what the technology cannot reliably know, infer or decide by itself.

This chapter examines AI limitations as professional constraints on diplomatic judgement. It focuses on data limitations and information quality; cultural, contextual and linguistic nuance; hallucination and verification; translation errors; operational consequences; and institutional barriers to adoption. The argument is deliberately measured. AI should not be portrayed as unsuitable for diplomacy. Survey respondents repeatedly describe efficiency gains, better drafting support and faster access to information. At the same time, their comments show a consistent awareness that diplomatic work cannot be reduced to retrieval, prediction or elegant wording. The most important limitation of AI is not that it sometimes makes mistakes, but that it can make mistakes in a form that looks authoritative.

***Figure 3.1  The chapter’s core process argument***

![][image7]

*Source: Authors’ synthesis based on attached project sources and survey findings.*

# **3.1 Data Limitations and Information Quality**

AI systems are only as useful as the information they can access, the assumptions they inherit and the context in which their output is read. In diplomatic work, information quality is especially difficult because relevant knowledge is often fragmented across official cables, internal minutes, public reporting, informal networks and institutional memory. A general-purpose model may provide a confident answer based on public information while missing the unpublished context that actually determines a ministry’s position. This is why data limitation is not merely a technical issue. It affects whether an AI-assisted brief understands the difference between what is publicly knowable, what is internally known and what is politically sayable.

The International AI Safety Report 2026 notes that the evidence base for AI risks remains uneven and that real-world performance can differ from controlled evaluation settings (International AI Safety Report, 2026). This matters for diplomacy because officials often ask questions about fast-moving issues for which the available public record is incomplete or contested. A system that has not been updated, that draws disproportionately from a particular information environment, or that lacks access to official sources may produce an answer that is coherent but misaligned with national interest. The limitation is not only wrong data, but missing data that the user may not know is missing.

Data integration also creates a second problem: inference. Wang et al. (2025) show that modern multimodal systems can combine textual, visual, geospatial and structured data in ways that reveal hidden relationships and sensitive operational information. In diplomatic practice, this cuts both ways. AI can help analysts connect scattered signals, but it can also tempt them to overinterpret weak associations or to merge datasets that were never intended to be read together. Where diplomatic information concerns national positions, consular cases or negotiation priorities, data quality must therefore include provenance, classification and purpose, not only factual accuracy.

# **3.2 Cultural, Contextual and Linguistic Nuance**

Diplomacy often works through what is not said directly. Tone, timing, hierarchy, venue, order of names, choice of verb and even punctuation can signal recognition, distance, displeasure or restraint. AI systems can reproduce diplomatic phrasing, but they do not possess lived diplomatic judgement. They may learn patterns from public documents, yet remain unable to know why a phrase is acceptable in one setting and inflammatory in another. This limitation is particularly important for Malaysia and other middle powers that operate across different linguistic, legal and cultural environments. A phrase that sounds neutral in English may carry a different history in Bahasa Melayu, Arabic, Mandarin, French or the diplomatic language of a regional forum.

Dato’ Mohd Suhaimi Jaafar captured this limitation in practical terms when discussing AI-assisted drafting. His concern was not simply that the machine might produce poor English, but that it may fail to read the layers of diplomatic language:

*“AI ni dia tak boleh nak read layers, you know... The choice of words tu macam-macam dia bagi, tapi dalam nuansanya tak berapa betul, dalam konteks is different.”1*

He then gave the example of references to Myanmar. In one setting, a general model might offer a politically charged label such as “military junta”. In ASEAN diplomatic parlance, however, the expression “Myanmar authorities” may be used to preserve a particular form of engagement. The difference is not cosmetic. It reflects institutional convention, political calculation and the need to maintain room for negotiation. This is the kind of context that cannot be delegated to autocomplete.

The survey findings echo this concern. Thirty-five of the 64 responses were coded for problems of context, tone, language or nuance. Respondents described AI-generated work as “generic”, “robotic”, “business-like”, “too polished” or lacking “diplomatic sensitivity and judgement”. Several also noted that AI can miss national positioning by reproducing Western assumptions. These comments point to a professional boundary: AI can assist with structure and vocabulary, but the diplomat must decide whether the language fits the audience, institutional voice and political context.

# **3.3 Reliability, Hallucinations and the Verification Problem**

Hallucination is the most visible reliability problem associated with generative AI, but it should be understood broadly. In diplomatic settings, a hallucination may appear as a fabricated citation, an outdated office-holder, a non-existent treaty provision, an invented quotation, a misleading translation or a plausible but false account of another state’s position. The danger is increased by fluency. Unlike a visibly incomplete note, an AI-generated paragraph often looks finished. It may therefore move through a workflow unless someone has the expertise and time to question it.

The International AI Safety Report 2026 observes that reliability failures may only appear in real-world use and that current mitigations, including retrieval-augmented generation and fine-tuning for factuality, can reduce but not eliminate failure rates in critical settings (International AI Safety Report, 2026). In high-stakes work, this means a model should not be judged only by whether it usually performs well. The relevant question is whether the institution can identify when it fails. NIST’s Generative AI Profile similarly treats trustworthiness as a lifecycle risk-management problem rather than a one-off accuracy score (Autio et al., 2024).

Survey data reinforce the importance of verification. Forty-seven of 64 respondents mentioned accuracy, hallucination, verification, unreliable sources or factual errors somewhere in their open-ended answers. This was not a marginal concern among sceptics; many of the same respondents also valued AI for speed and productivity. Their position is better described as conditional acceptance: use AI, but check it. This is a mature professional instinct. It recognises that the purpose of verification is not to slow innovation, but to prevent speed from outrunning judgement.

Ambassador Zamshari Shaharan made the same point in terms of prior knowledge. After describing how AI can support strategic communication, he emphasised that officers still need the background knowledge of foreign policy to verify outputs:

*“A combination of that knowledge, prior knowledge, and the technology, to me, is important.”2*

The implication is that AI literacy cannot be separated from substantive diplomatic literacy. Prompting skills are helpful, but they do not replace country knowledge, legal awareness, regional familiarity or institutional memory. A weak prompt may produce weak output; a strong prompt in the hands of a user without context may still produce work that sounds convincing but lacks diplomatic reliability.

***Table 3.1  AI limitations and diplomatic safeguards***

| AI limitation | Diplomatic consequence | Practical safeguard |
| ----- | ----- | ----- |
| Incomplete or outdated data | Briefs may miss recent developments, private channels or current national positions. | Use approved source sets, date checks and named document owners. |
| Loss of nuance | Wording may misread protocol, cultural expectation or regional diplomatic parlance. | Require human review by desk officers and language/context specialists. |
| Hallucination | Invented facts, citations or legal references may enter decision chains. | Use source verification, citation checks and “no-source, no-use” rules. |
| Translation errors | Literal translation may alter legal meaning, tone or formality. | Back-translate high-stakes texts and review with bilingual officers. |
| Institutional misfit | Tools may not align with classification, workflow or ministry systems. | Adopt secure platforms, clear SOPs and role-specific training. |

*Source: Authors’ synthesis based on survey responses, interview data and attached technical sources.*

# **3.4 Translation and Interpretation Errors**

Translation is one of the most attractive AI use cases for diplomats because multilingual work is time-sensitive and resource-intensive. AI can rapidly generate first drafts, compare alternative phrasings and assist officers who are not fully confident in a working language. Yet diplomatic translation is not only lexical substitution. It involves register, legal effect, cultural reference and institutional style. A literal rendering may be grammatically correct but politically imprecise. A phrase that is courteous in one language may sound evasive, weak or unnecessarily severe in another.

The limitation is especially acute when translation interacts with official terminology. In diplomatic notes, treaties, communiques and statements, a term may carry accumulated meaning from previous negotiations. A model may choose a more common word because it appears statistically likely, while the institution requires a specific term because it preserves continuity or avoids a legal concession. This is why translation and interpretation errors should not be treated as minor editing issues. They can alter the substance of a position.

The OECD AI Capability Indicators underline that AI capabilities should be assessed against different human abilities, including language, social interaction, problem solving and metacognition, rather than assumed as a single general competence (OECD, 2025\). For diplomacy, this distinction matters. A system may be strong at producing fluent language but weaker at recognising why one diplomatic formulation should be retained over another. Similarly, UNESCO’s guidance on generative AI stresses the need for human validation and capacity development when such systems are used in education and research (UNESCO, 2023\). In foreign ministries, that validation must be tied to the professional stakes of language.

A practical approach is to treat AI translation as an initial layer in a longer review chain. Low-stakes internal summaries may be translated quickly, with spot checks. High-stakes texts, by contrast, require bilingual review, comparison with previous official formulations and, where necessary, legal scrutiny. The aim is not to deny the usefulness of AI translation. It is to recognise that the convenience of instant language cannot replace the responsibility of official expression.

# **3.5 Operational Consequences of Technical Limitations**

Technical limitations become operational when they affect workflow, timing and accountability. A model that generates inaccurate information may require additional checking; a tool that cannot access secure data may produce incomplete summaries; a platform that is not approved for confidential material may be unusable for the most important tasks; a translation system that produces awkward phrasing may save minutes at the drafting stage but cost hours in review. These are not abstract defects. They shape whether AI becomes a trusted institutional tool or a private workaround used unevenly by individual officers.

Several survey respondents described this tension. Officers valued AI for summarising long documents, preparing drafts, refining language and speeding up research, yet repeatedly noted that outputs require careful checking. Some observed that the extra step of verifying facts can reduce the time saved. Others noted that official AI tools may be limited by security settings or insufficiently adapted to ministry-specific formats. These comments suggest that the operational value of AI depends less on the existence of a tool than on whether the tool fits real diplomatic workflows.

Operational consequences also include uneven expectations. If AI makes some documents faster to produce, senior leaders may expect faster turnaround even where the work still requires human judgement. A respondent noted that workplace demand for quantity has increased, while another observed that expectations had “exponentially increased”. This is an underappreciated limitation: AI can accelerate the production of text without accelerating the formation of judgement. If institutions treat speed as the main measure of productivity, they risk rewarding quick but shallow outputs.

For this reason, the operational question is not simply “Can AI do this task?” A better question is: “What kind of human review does this task require after AI assistance?” Routine grammar checking, formatting and basic summarisation may need light review. Policy analysis, negotiation advice and crisis communication require deeper verification and accountability. The UK AI Safety Institute’s open-source Inspect platform illustrates the broader policy direction: AI systems need structured evaluation tools that allow users and institutions to test performance rather than assume it (Department for Science, Innovation and Technology & AI Safety Institute, 2024).

# **3.6 Institutional and Technical Barriers to Adoption**

The final limitation lies not in the model but in the institution around it. A foreign ministry may encourage innovation yet lack secure infrastructure, clear rules, role-specific training or access to appropriate tools. This gap was evident in the survey. On the quantitative items, only 15 of 64 respondents agreed or strongly agreed that procedures for using AI applications within the organisation were clear and systematic, while 31 disagreed or strongly disagreed. Only 13 agreed or strongly agreed that they had access to expert guidance and the documentation necessary to operate AI systems effectively, while 22 disagreed or strongly disagreed. These figures show a readiness gap between enthusiasm for AI and the operational support needed to use it safely.

***Figure 3.2  Survey-coded hurdles to AI integration***

![][image8]

*Source: Authors’ coding of open-ended survey responses, Survey for Diplomats: Innovating Diplomacy, n \= 64\.*

The open-ended responses reinforce the same pattern. Fifty-four of 64 respondents mentioned training, literacy, guidelines, prompting or support; 35 mentioned tools, infrastructure or access; and 50 raised confidentiality, security or data-sensitivity concerns. These categories overlap because diplomats do not experience them separately. A secure tool is of limited value without training. Training is incomplete without guidance on classified information. A guideline is ineffective if officers cannot access an approved platform. The barrier is therefore systemic: AI adoption requires policy, technology, skills and culture to move together.

Ambassador Zamshari’s interview points to the same solution: training that is practical, shared and connected to the actual work of officers. He observed that awareness cannot be built simply by announcing that AI exists. Officers need to understand hallucination, prompting, source limits and the boundary between personal and official use. His conclusion was direct:

*“I think, tak ada jalan lain but training. You need to do training.”3*

Institutional readiness also requires clarity about what should not be automated. The Ministry of Science, Technology and Innovation’s National Guidelines on AI Governance and Ethics place responsible AI within principles such as fairness, reliability, privacy, transparency and accountability (Ministry of Science, Technology and Innovation Malaysia, 2024). For diplomacy, these principles must be translated into operating rules: what may be entered into an AI system, what must remain offline, who verifies output, and who accepts responsibility for decisions informed by AI. Without such rules, adoption will remain uneven and cautious officers may either avoid useful tools or use them informally without adequate safeguards.

# **Conclusion**

The limitations of AI in diplomatic practice are not reasons to retreat from innovation. They are reasons to innovate with greater discipline. AI can help diplomats search, draft, summarise, translate, compare and prepare. It can widen the range of materials considered and reduce the burden of routine text production. Yet it cannot carry the responsibility of representation, cannot reliably infer tacit context, and cannot know when an apparently efficient phrase undermines a carefully balanced position.

The chapter has shown that AI limitations travel through several layers. They begin with incomplete or uneven data, become visible in problems of nuance, reliability and translation, and then appear operationally as verification burden, workflow mismatch and uneven institutional readiness. The survey findings demonstrate that diplomats are not rejecting AI; rather, they are asking for the conditions that would make its use professionally safe: training, secure tools, clear guidance, source verification and human oversight.

The way forward is a verification-centred model of AI adoption. Low-risk administrative uses can be encouraged, but sensitive diplomatic work should pass through a structured loop: define the task, identify approved sources, test cultural and linguistic context, verify factual claims, review translation and ensure that final judgement remains human. In this model, AI literacy is not a technical add-on. It becomes part of diplomatic literacy itself.
